Finding Your Place in Highlands Ranch

Here's what I heard from you

Your search is about how the home and the neighborhood work together.

You loved your time in Ken Caryl before having kids. Now you're considering a return from the Chicago area, with two boys ages five and three. You want to picture the day-to-day: trails close by, strong schools, a welcoming community, and enough room for family life and two separate workspaces.

01 · The house

Three bedrooms + two offices

Ideally 2,500 or more finished square feet, but layout matters more than a strict cutoff. We'll consider smaller homes when the bedrooms, workspaces, and common areas genuinely function well.

02 · The budget

Looking across the full range

Your questionnaire originally identified $550,000–$700,000, and I still have that in mind. Since you’ve now chosen homes to see up to $800,000, I’m treating that as our practical search range for now. We’ll judge each home by how well it works for you and whether it represents good value—not by which end of the range it falls in.

03 · Family life

Trails, schools, and belonging

Proximity to walking and biking routes, parks, recreation, and other families matters. We'll pay attention to the feel of individual streets, not just neighborhood reputations.

04 · The yard

Useful, not necessarily enormous

A decent place to play and spend time outside matters, but a larger yard is not worth giving up the better location or a functional interior. Usability counts more than acreage.

A quick note about price: Your questionnaire originally listed $550,000–$700,000, and now we’re looking at homes you’ve selected up to $800,000. Jenny, you also mentioned up to $850,000 when we spoke on the phone—did I hear that correctly? It’s completely normal for the price range to change as you learn what’s available, even several times. For now, I’m treating about $800,000 as our working search ceiling, with no pressure to go higher. Just tell me whenever you want to change course, in either direction, and I’ll adapt.
One thing I want us to keep testing: Can we find three comfortable bedrooms and two spaces where you can actually take calls or close a door? A loft, flex room, or finished basement can sometimes solve the problem better than another formal bedroom.

Your questionnaire originally gave a $550,000–$700,000 range and a tentative summer move. Our working search now reflects the homes you’ve actually chosen to see, while the $850,000 figure remains something I want to confirm.

Orientation

Highlands Ranch is four different ways of living inside one community.

Westridge, Northridge, Southridge, and Eastridge are useful starting points. Each contains smaller subdivisions with their own architecture, lot sizes, street character, and neighborhood feel. For you, I wouldn't eliminate any ridge prematurely; I would use them to make a more focused tour.

Westridge

Foothills proximity, access toward Ken Caryl and Chatfield, Town Center, and great family recreation.

Northridge

Central convenience, established streets, varied homes and floor plans, and multiple routes toward Denver.

Southridge

Backcountry trails, Daniels Park, neighborhood programming in some subdivisions, and a broad range of houses.

Eastridge

Easy access to Lone Tree and the DTC, indoor family pools, and higher-elevation mountain views in some pockets.

Most Highlands Ranch homeowners are in the Highlands Ranch Community Association (HRCA), which maintains four recreation centers and offers access to the 8,200-acre Backcountry Wilderness Area, including approximately 26 miles of trails for members. The standard annual assessment shown on many of the properties in our dataset is about $696, but individual neighborhoods can have additional assessments. Explore HRCA recreation.

Westridge

Closest to the foothills—and perhaps closest to what you loved about Ken Caryl.

Westridge deserves an early look. Access west toward Chatfield and Ken Caryl is convenient, and the Town Center area gives you everyday amenities, restaurants, and community events. If trail access is a central piece of why you're returning to Colorado, this is an easy place to begin.

What family life looks like

Westridge Recreation Center: My favorite outdoor pool of the four for little kids, with zero-depth water and slides, plus indoor aquatics, a track, and fitness amenities. Redstone Park has fields, a playground, a pond, and open space. Civic Green Park puts you right by Town Center with a splash feature, playground, and community gathering space.

For biking and walking, the western side provides especially appealing links to the broader trail network and easier drives toward Chatfield State Park.

What I would watch

A house here with a well-located office or finished-basement flex space could be a great match. I'd be less concerned with modest yard dimensions if the walk to parks and trails is excellent.

Foothills accessChatfieldYoung-kid pools
Northridge

Established neighborhoods, central access, and lots of floor-plan variety.

Northridge has a good mix of 1980s, 1990s, and newer homes, which means there are often multiple approaches to the same budget: a more updated smaller home, or a larger home with room to improve. Streets and lot configurations vary, so the subdivision matters more than the broad label.

What family life looks like

Northridge Recreation Center offers indoor and outdoor aquatics and a strong racquet-sports focus. Northridge Park, near the recreation center, and Toepfer Park bring playground and open-field options close to established neighborhoods. Access toward the city can be flexible using Broadway, University, Colorado Boulevard, and C-470 depending on the address.

Why it makes the shortlist

Good hunting ground for homes with a den or converted bedroom plus a basement retreat. That combination could give you two offices while keeping three dedicated bedrooms upstairs.

Central locationEstablished streetsLayout variety
Southridge

Backcountry access and family-focused neighborhoods.

Southridge offers proximity to the Backcountry Wilderness Area and Daniels Park, along with a wide range of house sizes and ages. Firelight and The Hearth are two neighborhoods I'd keep in the mix: both show up repeatedly in our price-band data, and some streets offer a real sense of neighborhood activity.

What family life looks like

Southridge Recreation Center has a current channel, leisure pools, an outdoor pool, courts, and fitness amenities. I like its aquatic setup for children moving into the elementary-school years. Dad Clark Park has a playground, fields, and places to gather. Backcountry trails provide an entirely different outdoor experience from the neighborhood sidewalk loop.

Some subdivisions carry an additional HOA beyond HRCA, sometimes with neighborhood events or services. We'd review the actual cost and benefit for every property.

What matters here

Look for flexible upstairs lofts and finished basements. A little more space or a better floor plan may be a stronger long-term choice than paying a premium for cosmetic updates.

Backcountry trailsFirelightThe Hearth
Eastridge

Great family facilities, with Lone Tree just next door.

Eastridge offers convenience to Lone Tree shopping, dining, and I-25 access. The higher elevation in some areas also produces attractive westward mountain-view opportunities, even though you're physically farther from the foothills.

What family life looks like

Eastridge Recreation Center has my favorite indoor pool for young children: zero-entry and smaller-slide features make it especially manageable for a three-year-old, with plenty for a five-year-old as well. Highland Heritage Regional Park offers playgrounds, athletic fields, and community activities.

Why I'd include it

You might find better everyday convenience without sacrificing trails and recreation. It also naturally extends the search into the established neighborhoods of Lone Tree—but Lone Tree homeowners don't automatically have HRCA privileges.

Lone TreeFamily poolsDTC access
Beyond the four ridges

Two nearby alternatives I'd absolutely keep open.

Lone Tree

A practical extension of the search

Established Lone Tree neighborhoods can offer family-friendly streets, parks, and quick access to shopping and regional trails. The trade-off is sometimes less house for the money or different recreation access. Our MLS sample includes several properties under $800,000 with four or five bedrooms and workable finished space.

My view: worth watching, especially where the house configuration works. Judge the precise neighborhood and any HOA separately.

TrailMark at Chatfield

The Ken Caryl comparison

TrailMark is particularly interesting because of your history in Ken Caryl. Its setting near the foothills and Chatfield, surrounding open space, and trail-oriented feel may give you some of the Colorado lifestyle you're looking to recover. It's in Littleton and served by Jeffco Public Schools, rather than Douglas County schools.

My view: a strong lifestyle candidate. Inventory inside your price range is thinner in this particular export, so let's evaluate every well-suited option carefully. TrailMark has its own HOA and recreation-district arrangements, separate from HRCA. TrailMark community information.

Trade-off to test in person: TrailMark may win on the feeling of the setting. Highlands Ranch may win on access to four recreation centers and a broader supply of houses with flexible layouts. Neither is automatically better; it depends on what a particular home delivers.
Schools and family life

Your boys are at an age when the daily routine matters more than a school ranking.

With children ages five and three, I'd look at elementary assignment, preschool or early-childhood options, after-school programs, and the route from your front door to the places you'll use all week. A playground five minutes away and a trail you can enter without getting into the car are meaningful advantages.

Public schools

Highlands Ranch is largely served by Douglas County School District; TrailMark is in Jeffco Public Schools. Highlands Ranch elementary consolidations took effect for the 2026–27 school year, so older MLS school fields may be out of date.

Preschool & enrichment

HRCA hosts preschool and children's activities, including programming at Westridge and other centers. Nature preschool and enrichment opportunities in the Backcountry are worth exploring.

Community connections

Neighborhood parks, rec-center programs, youth sports, pools, school communities, and local events can help you find other families and build routines quickly after a move.

School changes worth knowing about

For fall 2026, Golden Ridge Elementary combined the former Eldorado and Saddle Ranch schools; Mountain Peak combined Heritage and Summit View; and Silver Spruce combined Acres Green and Fox Creek. When an address interests you, we'll check its current assignment directly against district address records rather than relying only on listing copy. Douglas County schools · Jeffco schools.

Market update · November 22, 2026

A practical look at the market across your search range.

I reviewed two supplied MLS exports for single-family homes in Highlands Ranch and the nearby search areas: 185 records in the $550,000–$700,000 band and 222 records in the $700,000–$825,000 band. To make the comparison fair, both price ranges use exactly the same measures and status definitions. These are filtered snapshots, not the whole market.

Homes from $550,000–$700,000

This range remains relevant, especially if a home delivers the space and layout you need at a lower cost. The MLS snapshot covers single-family properties in our search areas, not the entire regional market.

Days on market are the MLS export's ‘Days’ values, shown separately for closed sales and currently active homes. Active days measure time on market so far; closed days describe the sold group and should not be interpreted as time to closing. Sale-to-original-ask excludes the one lower-range closing without an original asking price. One coming-soon listing in each export is excluded from active and pending counts.

Across both price bands, there are homes with enough square footage and bedroom count to work. The key is identifying truly usable space for two separate offices, an enjoyable neighborhood, and a yard that meets your needs. We’ll weigh the floor plan and condition against the price rather than setting a rigid lower-band preference.

How I'd interpret it for your search

Buyers can negotiate—but selectively.

In both price bands, the median sold home closed below its original asking price, and about two-thirds of current active listings have already reduced asking prices. That points to opportunities, especially for overpriced or longer-listed homes, but negotiation depends on the specific house.

Good homes still move.

Even with longer-running active inventory, the median closed sale went under contract after 17 reported market days. Some sold in just two or three days. A home that's well-priced for its condition and location may not leave much room to wait.

Concessions matter.

Seller concessions were reported for 70 of 120 closed sales in the original-budget group and 101 of 156 in the higher-budget group. Concessions can help with closing costs or financing, but we should compare the total economics rather than treating the sale price alone as the whole picture.

More square footage is possible.

The median closed home had approximately 2,954 finished square feet. There are multiple current examples under $800,000 with 2,500–3,500+ finished square feet. Your space goal is realistic within the budget, provided the layout and condition fit.

My strategy: We’ll consider homes across your working price range. For each one, we’ll review comparable sales, price history, condition, and how well it meets your bedroom, office, and lifestyle priorities. We can negotiate when the facts support it; we won’t rule out a great fit simply because it costs more than your original questionnaire range.

Prepared by Jake Freedle and Freedle & Associates. This guide compares neighborhoods and homes throughout your working price range, with practical guidance for your family.

The plan

Let's see the neighborhoods and a handful of different home styles.

Since you'll be in town November 23–25, I'd rather use that time as an orientation trip than try to maximize the number of houses we see. Visiting a few contrasting neighborhoods and home layouts should help answer the questions that photos can't.

01 · Feel the place

Spend time in a western Highlands Ranch neighborhood, a more central or eastern pocket, and TrailMark if scheduling allows. Look at nearby trails, playgrounds, and everyday conveniences.

02 · Stress-test the layout

For each house, actually assign the bedrooms, two offices, play space, and storage. We'll notice quickly whether a house lives bigger or smaller than its square footage suggests.

03 · Let value guide timing

We’ll look seriously at the homes you’ve chosen up to about $800,000, while keeping lower-priced options in the mix when they fit. You can narrow or widen the range whenever you prefer.

My biggest takeaway: We’re exploring homes up to approximately $800,000 because that’s where your actual selections have taken us. I’ll keep looking for strong value at every price point, with the emphasis on three bedrooms, two workable offices, family amenities, and a location that makes you excited to return to Colorado.
